title: Fe-based metallic glasses as efficient oxygen scavengers

paper_content.abstract: Ubiquitous oxygen drives degradation, spoilage, and side reactions, making oxygen scavenging essential for materials preservation and reaction stabilization. However, conventional oxygen scavengers exhibit limited oxygen removal rates and capacities far below their theoretical maximums, wasting resources while lagging behind industry needs. Here, we report Fe-based metallic glasses as efficient oxygen scavengers, achieving oxygen removal rates 1–4 orders of magnitude higher than conventional systems. In FeSiB metallic glass, Fe oxidation synergistically activates Si, delivering a 24-hour oxygen removal capacity of 1.439 L g-1—reaching the Fe-based theoretical limit—and a 48-hour capacity of 1.596 L g-1, surpassing it. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the amorphous structure significantly lowers the oxygen adsorption energy barrier and facilitates O–O bond cleavage. Moreover, the generated self-reinforcing microdomains mediate O2/H2O transport via robust autocatalytic cycling. These results highlight a promising strategy for oxygen potential control and suggest a possible paradigm for catalytic applications.
paper_content.introduction:
Though essential to life, the ubiquity of oxygen drives unwanted reactions, making effective scavenging crucial for food and pharmaceutical preservation, cultural relics conservation, and chemical synthesis1-5. Fe-based scavengers, the most prevalent type, can remove oxygen through a redox reaction that proceeds in electrolyte-containing environments1,6. Theoretically, 1 g of iron can remove oxygen from approximately 1566 mL of air at 298 K; however, the actual performance falls far short7, reflecting decades of stagnant efficiency and significant resource waste. Moreover, the performance of conventional scavengers remains fundamentally limited by three key challenges: intrinsically low oxygen adsorption activity, surface passivation due to oxidation product accumulation, and a sharp decline in reaction kinetics under low-oxygen conditions—a limitation widely deemed unavoidable6-11. These constraints hinder their use in demanding applications like gas purification and catalyst protection.

Metallic glasses (MGs) are known for their exceptional mechanical and functional properties12-16, with Fe-based MGs being particularly promising for large-scale applications due to their good glass-forming ability and low cost17. While they have been widely used as soft-magnetic materials, their potential in chemical reactions remains largely unexplored.

In this study, we report the use of Fe-based MGs as oxygen scavengers, achieving unmatched efficiency that far exceeds conventional materials. Fe78Si9B13 (FeSiB) MG exhibits excellent oxygen scavenging performance even at a low temperature of 278 K, whereas conventional Fe-based oxygen scavengers are nearly ineffective. Kinetic studies reveal a self-accelerating oxygen scavenging process, while density functional theory (DFT) calculations show that FeSiB MG possesses significantly lower oxygen adsorption energy barrier than crystalline iron. Moreover, the formation of a unique coupled structure—comprising moisture-retaining and adsorption zones—endows the system with strong autocatalytic behavior. These features overcome long-standing limitations of conventional systems and enable exceptional performance under low-oxygen conditions. Their marked superiority and low cost over existing benchmarks position them as enabling materials for next-generation oxygen-sensitive applications (Fig. 1a).
paper_content.results:
Accelerating oxygen removal kinetics
To evaluate oxygen removal performance, we compared FeSiB MG, pure iron, and reduced iron (commonly used in industry) powders in 500 mL sealed air under saline and non-saline conditions. Using 2 g samples with matched volumetric particle sizes (Supplementary Fig. 1), we added either 1 g ultrapure water (non-saline) or 1 wt% NaCl solution (saline), plus 0.8 g diatomite as a moisture-retaining agent. This controlled setup enabled direct performance comparisons under identical conditions.

Fig. 1b,c demonstrates the superior oxygen removal kinetics of FeSiB MG. Even under non-saline conditions, it achieved complete oxygen removal in just 11.9 hours, showing high reactivity (Fig. 1b). The complete oxygen removal time here is defined as the period required for the oxygen concentration <0.05%, corresponding to >99.7% oxygen removal. In contrast, pure iron and reduced iron showed much slower kinetics and activity decay after 4 hours due to surface passivation. Reduced iron outperformed pure iron owing to its porous structure with much larger surface area. Adding 1 wt% NaCl significantly enhanced the oxygen removal performance of all three materials (Fig. 1c), confirming the role of electrolyte in promoting electron transfer. FeSiB MG achieved a shorter removal time of 5.6 hours, while pure and reduced iron powders still failed to reach complete removal within 24 hours, even under optimized conditions.

In this reaction system, given the ample metal supply and continuous oxygen depletion, oxygen removal kinetics can be described using the pseudo-first-order kinetic model18-20, the apparent rate constant k can be obtained by Equation (1):
k = -ln(C/C0)/t (1)
where C represents the real-time oxygen concentration, C0 is the initial oxygen concentration, and t is the reaction time. Using this equation, the data from Fig. 1b,c were replotted in Fig. 1d,e, where the curve slope at each point reflects the instantaneous reaction rate.

As shown in Fig. 1d, the -ln(C/C0) curve for FeSiB MG displays exponential-type growth, indicating a continuously accelerating reaction rate that deviates from traditional kinetics. In contrast, pure iron and reduced iron show curves that level off, reflecting declining activity. Under saline conditions, FeSiB MG still follows an accelerating trend with a steeper slope (Fig. 1e), confirming electrolyte-enhanced kinetics. Meanwhile, the curves for pure iron and reduced iron become nearly linear, aligning with pseudo-first-order behavior.

Differentiating the curves in Fig. 1d,e yields Fig. 1f,g, where the vertical coordinate represents the instantaneous oxygen removal rate. FeSiB MG shows a much higher initial rate than the two crystalline iron powders, confirming its intrinsically high reactivity. All materials exhibit a slight rate dip in the first 1–2 hours, likely due to initial oxide formation hindering internal oxidation. Uniquely, FeSiB MG displays accelerating kinetics—starting after 3 hours without electrolyte, and as early as 1 hour with electrolyte. This suggests a strong autocatalytic effect during oxygen removal. In such reactions, a product also acts as a catalyst, causing the rate to increase as the reaction proceeds—as seen in acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis and liquid-phase crystallization21,22. For comparison, pure iron shows a continuous rate decline to near zero under both conditions. Reduced iron behaves similarly under non-saline conditions, but under saline conditions, it displays a V-shaped curve: the rate drops sharply in the first 2 hours, then gradually rises. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) results in Supplementary Fig. 2 show that Fe3O4 and FeO(OH) are simultaneously formed during the reaction. At the early stage (2 hours), Fe3O4 dominates, leading to a relatively low oxygen removal rate. With continued reaction, the FeO(OH) phase progressively increases and becomes pronounced at 6 and 8 hours, giving rise to the V-shaped variation in Fig. 1g. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images shown in Supplementary Fig. 3, together with the energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) maps in Supplementary Fig. 4, further corroborate the result.

Record-high oxygen removal capacity
Fig. 2a compares the oxygen removal time and percentage for the three materials, underscoring the superior performance of FeSiB MG. To quantify this, we integrated the instantaneous rate curves from Fig. 1f,g and divided by the reaction time to obtain the average rate ka. As shown in Fig. 2b, under non-saline conditions, the ka of FeSiB MG is 60 times that of pure iron and 41 times that of reduced iron powder; under saline conditions, it remains 40 and 9 times higher, respectively.

Besides reaction rate, oxygen removal capacity is another key metric for evaluating scavenger performance. To assess it more accurately, we used 0.5 g of sample and increased the air volume to 1200 mL to ensure sufficient moisture and oxygen. Based on their iron mass fraction (FeSiB MG: 91.7%, pure iron: 100%, reduced iron: 98.8%), the theoretical maximum oxygen removal capacities at 298 K are 1.436, 1.566, and 1.547 L, respectively.

Fig. 2c compares the equivalent oxygen removal capacities—defined as the volume of air from which oxygen is removed—at 12, 24, and 48 hours, relative to theoretical limits. In practical use, performance within 12 hours is most critical. In 12 hours, 1 g of FeSiB can remove oxygen from 1.045 L of air, approaching its theoretical maximum and far exceeding pure iron (0.149 L) and reduced iron (0.440 L). After 24 hours, FeSiB reaches 1.439 L g-1, reaching its Fe-based theoretical limit, and further increases to 1.596 L g-1 at 48 hours—surpassing even the theoretical limit of pure iron (1.566 L g-1). The highly reactive Fe atoms in FeSiB promote the synergistic involvement of Si in the reaction, a phenomenon first reported here (Supplementary Fig. 5).

To comprehensively compare material performance, a radar chart (Fig. 2d) was constructed using ka, and weight-, cost-, and area-normalized equivalent oxygen removal capacities (12- and 24-hours). Given the porous nature of reduced iron powder, specific surface areas were measured via the BET method. FeSiB MG outperforms reduced iron powder across all metrics, delivering much higher oxygen removal rates and capacities despite having less than one-tenth of the surface area. Owing to its low material and processing costs, FeSiB MG also shows superior cost-effectiveness—approximately 2.3× higher than reduced iron based on 12-hour performance (Supplementary Fig. 6). Moreover, as Fe-based MGs do not require specific formability, thickness, or magnetic properties for use as oxygen scavengers, processing costs are expected to decrease further.

The oxygen removal performance of FeSiB MG can be further improved. Pre-reacting 2.1 g of FeSiB powder with oxygen to consume 0.1 g significantly enhances its activity. This modified material is referred to as pre-reacted FeSiB (see Methods for details). Additionally, atomized amorphous powders Fe78Si9B13 (denoted as FeSiB-2) and Fe77.3Si6.3B13.9C2.6 (FeSiBC) with smaller particle sizes show markedly improved performance, removing >99.7% of oxygen from 500 mL of air within just 1.6 and 2.0 hours, respectively. Such rapid kinetics demonstrate its potential for oxygen potential regulation.

Fig. 2e compares the oxygen removal rates of Fe-based MG scavengers from this study with various reported systems8,11,23-30. For reliable comparison, all rates here were calculated as volume of oxygen removed per unit time and weight. The results show that Fe-based MGs outperform all others by 1-4 orders of magnitude in oxygen removal rate.

Low-temperature and long-term storage performance
In practical applications, Fe-based oxygen scavengers are typically operated within a temperature range of 288-303 K. For conventional reduced iron powders, decreasing temperature suppresses the reaction kinetics of oxygen consumption, rendering them largely ineffective below approximately 283 K. To systematically evaluate the low-temperature adaptability of FeSiB MG and reduced iron powder, comparative oxygen scavenging experiments were therefore conducted at 278 K.

As shown in Fig. 3a, the oxygen absorption performance of conventional reduced iron powder deteriorates substantially under low-temperature conditions: only about half of the oxygen is consumed within 24 h, which is insufficient to meet the preservation requirements in food and pharmaceutical packaging. In contrast, the FeSiB oxygen scavenger maintains a high oxygen removal rate at 278 K and is capable of completely depleting the oxygen in a sealed container within 15 h. These results demonstrate that the FeSiB MG scavenger effectively overcomes the low-temperature performance limitations inherent to conventional iron-based systems.

The kinetic fitting results in Fig. 3b further reveal that the FeSiB MG retains an autocatalytic reaction behavior even at low temperature, whereas no such characteristic is observed for reduced iron powder. This sustained autocatalytic feature under low-temperature conditions accounts for the superior oxygen removal performance and substantially broadens the applicable temperature window of Fe-based oxygen scavengers.

In addition to operational performance, long-term storage stability is a critical consideration for practical deployment, as oxygen scavengers are commonly stored in sealed environments for extended periods prior to use. To assess storage stability, the as-prepared FeSiB scavengers were sealed in 10 mL centrifuge tubes and stored at room temperature for 30 days before oxygen scavenging measurements were conducted. As shown in Fig. 3c, no noticeable degradation in oxygen removal performance is observed after storage, indicating that prolonged sealing does not induce surface passivation of the MG. This long-term retention of reactivity highlights the robustness of the FeSiB scavenger and underscores its suitability for applications requiring both low-temperature operability and extended shelf life.

Atomic-scale insights from DFT
To better understand the exceptional oxygen removal performance of FeSiB MG, we simulated the O2 molecule adsorption process on its surface in the presence of H2O molecules and compared it with that on the body-centered cubic (BCC) Fe(110) surface—the most stable and densely packed surface of BCC Fe31. Using climbing image-nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations based on DFT, we estimated the transition states and energy barriers for O2 adsorption. The energy barrier in the pure Fe case is 3.39 eV, while in the FeSiB MG case it is only 1.29 eV (Fig. 4a; transition states in Fig. 4b; full structures in Supplementary Fig. 7), indicating a much easier O2 adsorption process on FeSiB MG and explaining its superior oxygen removal activity.

We have also calculated the energy barriers of the O2 adsorption process by using the implicit solvent model to include the effect of the NaCl electrolyte. It should be noted that the possible specific effects of chloride ions were not considered in this model. The FeSiB MG still shows a lower energy barrier and therefore easier O2 adsorption (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Besides, the O2 adsorption process on the diamond-structured pure Si(111) surface and Si sites on the FeSiB MG surface were also calculated, with and without considering implicit solvation effects. The results show lower energy barriers of the O2 adsorption on both the pure Si and Si atom in FeSiB MG (see Supplementary Figs. 9-12 for more details), supporting that the Si can actively react with O2. However, in bulk crystalline Si, the formation of a surface Si oxide layer prevents the inner Si atoms from reacting with oxygen, whereas in FeSiB MG, the preferential oxidation of Fe promotes the oxidation of Si and maintains the exposure of active sites. The role of Si will be discussed in detail in the following section.

According to energy band theory, the adsorption process involves the hybridization of Fe 4s and 3d orbitals with O orbitals, forming bonding and antibonding states. This interaction leads to electron rearrangement, changes in charge density, bond breaking (O-O), and bond formation (Fe-O)32,33. Since the Fe 4s orbitals are broad in the energy and their projected density of states (PDOS) is much smaller than Fe 3d orbitals (see Supplementary Fig. 13), the primary effects arise from the hybridization between O and Fe 3d orbitals34. The overall energy change in this process can be effectively described by the Fe d-band center (see Methods section). An upward shift of the Fe d-band center strengthens the Fe–O interaction by reducing the occupation of Fe–O antibonding states, which facilitates electron transfer into the O antibonding orbitals, weakens the O–O bond, and ultimately promotes O2 dissociation35-38, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. This d-band center theory has been successful in describing transition metal surfaces39-42.

In our results, the PDOS for the 3d orbitals of surface Fe atoms before O2 adsorption was obtained, and the corresponding d-band centers were calculated (Fig. 4c). FeSiB MG shows a higher d-band center at -1.55 eV compared to -1.85 eV for pure Fe, which explains its stronger O2 adsorption. The pure Fe value closely matches the reported value of -1.80 eV43, confirming the result of our calculation. The higher d-band center of FeSiB MG is also confirmed in the calculation with implicit solvent model (Supplementary Fig. 8b). To further understand the stronger adsorption, the charge density difference around the O2 molecule in the initial states (Fig. 4d) is presented. For FeSiB MG, there is a decrease in charge density between the O atoms and an increase around them, indicating a stronger tendency for O-O bond breaking. In contrast, O2 on pure Fe shows a decrease in overall charge density with no significant O-O bond breaking, consistent with its lower d-band center and higher adsorption energy barrier. Overall, DFT calculations reveal a low energy barrier for O2 adsorption on FeSiB MG, explaining its exceptional oxygen removal activity on the atomic scale.

Origin of robust autocatalytic effect
Based on the experimental data shown in Figs. 1b and 1c, the correlation curves between the oxygen removal kinetics and the mass of reaction products under the two conditions were constructed (see Supplementary Figs. 15a,b). The evolution trends of these curves indicate that, the oxygen removal process exhibits a typical autocatalytic behavior, characterized by a rapid acceleration of the reaction rate with increasing product formation. To probe the mechanism of autocatalytic behavior, we analyzed the reacted composite powder under saline conditions. The reacted samples were washed with ethanol to remove loosely bound iron oxides and part of residual diatomite, then dried and characterized by XRD, as shown in Fig. 5a. Due to interference from diatomite and moisture, reliable and systematic information could not be readily obtained from operando XRD measurements; therefore, the reaction products were subjected to post-treatment.

XRD analysis reveals distinct oxidation behavior of FeSiB MG. The reaction products consist mainly of diatomite and residual amorphous phase. γ-FeO(OH) is identified as the primary oxidation product, though its weak diffraction intensity suggests poor adhesion to the MG matrix, with most oxides removed during washing. This facilitates continuous exposure of active sites, which is essential for sustained oxygen scavenging. Poor adhesion and easy spallation of FeO(OH)-type oxides are widely recognized and well documented in corrosion science and oxidation literature20,44. XRD pattern (Supplementary Fig. 16) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image (Supplementary Fig. 17) of the separated orange-red products further confirm γ-FeO(OH) as the dominant oxidation species. In contrast, pure iron and reduced iron exhibit markedly different oxidation behavior. Post-reaction XRD pattern shows dominant Fe3O4 along with minor γ-FeO(OH) and α-FeO(OH), indicating sluggish kinetics in crystalline iron that lead to incomplete oxidation and passivating Fe3O4 formation. These results underscore the fundamental contrast between FeSiB MG and crystalline iron. DFT calculations provide mechanistic insight: the strong oxygen adsorption and dissociation abilities of FeSiB enhance surface reactivity, enabling complete oxidation and suppressing Fe3O4 formation.

To elucidate the autocatalytic mechanism of FeSiB MG, we conducted microscopic characterization of the reacted powder. SEM and EDS mapping images (Fig. 5b-d) reveal a coupled microstructure of diatomite (cyan) and nano iron oxides (red) on the particle surface. This interfacial structure is key to enhanced oxygen removal. Such regions are characteristic of the post-reaction particles, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 18. BET analysis shows the oxidation products (including adhered diatomite) possess a high specific surface area of 121 m2 g-1, far exceeding that of pristine diatomite (1.65 m2 g-1; Supplementary Fig. 19). These findings, along with oxygen removal data, clarify the autocatalytic behavior of FeSiB MG.

As illustrated in Fig. 5e, the initial oxygen removal by FeSiB MG is driven by surface adsorption of O2 and H2O, with diatomite providing moisture to sustain the reaction. Over time, a nanoporous γ-FeO(OH) layer rapidly forms, coupling with diatomite to create a hierarchical interfacial structure. This architecture promotes reactant transport, prevents surface passivation to maintain active site exposure, and provides stable interfaces for electron transfer. As the reaction progresses, the evolving porous nano-oxide layer further refines the interface, underpinning the observed autocatalytic behavior. This stands in stark contrast to that of crystalline iron.

Autocatalytic reactions commonly show slow initial rates because of low product concentrations21,22. In contrast, FeSiB MG deviates fundamentally from this conventional pattern: its amorphous structure enables high intrinsic reactivity from the onset.

Prior studies show that Fe2+ and Fe3+ species in Fe(OH)2 and FeO(OH) can reorganize into Fe3O445, but FeSiB MG—with its superior oxygen adsorption and dissociation capabilities—undergoes complete oxidation, effectively avoiding Fe3O4 formation. Its highly adsorptive surface layer further promotes oxygen transport, ensuring full utilization of Fe. These findings align with reports linking Fe3O4 formation to Fe(OH)2 oxidation46 and its possible transformation into γ-FeO(OH) and α-FeO(OH) under suitable conditions47, offering a mechanistic basis for the distinct reactivity of FeSiB MG.

A simple experiment confirms the strong link between FeSiB MG’s autocatalytic effect and its surface structure. Pre-reacting the powder to form a dual-zone interface—comprising a water-retention zone and a strong adsorption zone—significantly enhanced oxygen removal, reducing the complete oxygen removal time from 5.6 to 3.5 hours (Supplementary Fig. 20).

Analysis of oxidation behavior
To elucidate the oxidation mechanism of the FeSiB MG oxygen scavenger, a series of controlled experiments was designed. Fig. 6a compares the Fe 2p3/2 X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra of the native oxide layers formed on FeSiB MG and pure Fe. The FeSiB sample exhibits a higher initial oxidation state of Fe, indicating a stronger intrinsic affinity for oxygen.

To isolate the contribution of Si, additional experiments were conducted in the absence of diatomite. Specifically, 2 g of FeSiB powder was mixed with 30 μL of 1 wt% NaCl solution and allowed to react under ambient air. After 1 h, an additional 30 μL of solution was introduced, and this procedure was repeated multiple times. Samples subjected to n cycles were denoted as FeSiB-Rn. The small volume of electrolyte was deliberately chosen to achieve micro-wetting without full immersion, ensuring that oxygen uptake occurred at the solid–gas–liquid interface rather than via bulk solution reactions. This condition is critical for effective oxygen scavenging.

XPS spectra were first detected for samples subjected to 10, 20, and 30 reaction cycles. The relative fractions of Si oxides and Fe oxides in the resulting surface oxide layers were quantified and compared with those of the native oxide on the as-prepared alloy, as well as with the nominal bulk composition. The XPS spectra of Si and Fe oxides are shown in Supplementary Figs. 21 and 22, respectively.

The results are summarized in Fig. 6b. Notably, the native oxide layer on FeSiB MG is already strongly enriched in Si oxides relative to the nominal composition, indicating a pronounced oxygen affinity of Si, in good agreement with the DFT predictions. More importantly, the Si-to-Fe oxide ratio increases monotonically with progressive oxidation. As shown in the XPS survey spectra in Supplementary Fig. 23, the signal corresponding to oxidized Si is clearly pronounced. This trend provides compelling evidence for the active participation of Si in the oxygen scavenging process; in the absence of a significant Si contribution, continued oxidation of Fe would be expected to yield a surface dominated by Fe oxides, thereby precluding any further increase in the relative Si content.

Figs. 6c and d show the XRD patterns of reacted FeSiB and pure Fe samples from the diatomite-free experiments. To exclude thermal effects, all samples were dried naturally at room temperature. In the FeSiB series, the diffraction features are weak due to the poor crystallinity of the oxidation products; nevertheless, the characteristic reflections of γ-FeO(OH) are discernible in the FeSiB-R20 sample. In contrast, for pure Fe, the formation of Fe3O4 is detected after only two reaction cycles. These observations are fully consistent with the above XRD results.

To further quantify the oxidation degree and Fe–O coordination environment in the FeSiB MG and pure Fe, synchrotron-based X-ray absorption measurements were performed on samples reacted for the same duration (5.5 h). Fig. 6e presents the Fe K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra of FeSiB before reaction, FeSiB after reaction, and reacted pure Fe. As the absorption edge position reflects the Fe oxidation state, the edge of reacted pure Fe (blue curve) is clearly shifted to lower energy relative to that of reacted FeSiB (red curve), confirming a lower average oxidation state. Moreover, the pronounced intensity differences highlighted by the red arrow indicate a higher oxidation degree in FeSiB MG.

Fig. 6f shows the corresponding extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra (phase shift not corrected) in R space, which provide insight into the local Fe–O coordination. Comparison of the pristine alloy (black) and reacted FeSiB (red) confirms that the post-reaction spectra are not significantly influenced by residual Fe coordination in the MG. The FeSiB scavenger exhibits a broadened first-shell Fe–O contribution (R ≈ 1.3–1.5 Å), accompanied by a weak, continuous second-shell feature (R ≈ 2.6–2.9 Å), while higher-shell contributions are largely suppressed. This coordination signature is characteristic of low-crystallinity Fe oxyhydroxide species closely resembling γ-FeO(OH).

In contrast, the crystalline Fe-based scavenger displays a different EXAFS profile, with a strong first-shell Fe–O peak at 1.1–1.5 Å and a pronounced second-shell feature at 2.6–2.9 Å, together with retained medium-intensity signals in the 3.5–4.5 Å range. These features are indicative of a mixed coordination environment dominated by Fe3O4, with additional contributions from FeO(OH). A weak feature at ~2.3 Å suggests a minor fraction of residual metallic Fe. Notably, the intensity observed around 1.1–1.2 Å does not correspond to an independent coordination shell but arises from the low-R extension of the first-shell Fe–O contribution, a common characteristic of Fe–O-based systems. This effect is intrinsic to both iron oxides and oxyhydroxides and is further influenced by phase shifts, window functions, and multiple-scattering contributions.

Taken together, the XANES and EXAFS results consistently demonstrate that Fe in the FeSiB MG is oxidized more readily and to a higher degree than in crystalline Fe, corroborating its superior oxygen scavenging capability.

Analysis of the contribution of Si
To evaluate the contribution of Si in the FeSiB MG, SEM observation was performed on the FeSiB-R20 sample prepared without diatomite to eliminate interference. As shown in Fig. 7a, the reacted FeSiB-R20 exhibits a highly porous surface morphology, with a large fraction of oxidation products appearing as delaminated or exfoliated features. The corresponding EDS elemental maps (Fig. 7b-e) acquired from the region highlighted in Fig. 7a show pronounced enrichment of Fe and O within the oxide layer, accompanied by a clear Si signal, confirming the involvement of Si in the oxidation process. The EDS spectrum (Fig. 7f) yields an average composition of Fe31.77Si2.74O65.49 (at%), corresponding to a Si-to-Fe atomic ratio of 8.62%, slightly lower than the nominal value of 11.54%. Assuming the oxidized Si is present as SiO2, the estimated contribution of Si to oxygen uptake reaches ~11.49% for controlled experiments without diatomite. Considering the presence of intermediate Si oxidation states, the actual contribution is expected to be close to but slightly lower than this value. It should be noted that the removal of diatomite in this experimental series may lead to minor variations in the apparent Si contribution compared with diatomite-containing systems. Nevertheless, these results unambiguously demonstrate the active role of Si in oxygen scavenging and provide a reasonable quantitative estimate of its contribution.

Raman and infrared spectroscopy were also employed to probe the oxidation behavior of Si (see Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25); however, their phase discriminability was limited. On one hand, the presence of Fe–Si and Fe–B bonding in the FeSiB alloy gives rise to multiple intrinsic vibrational features that complicate spectral assignment. On the other hand, the poor crystallinity of the oxidation products leads to significant peak broadening, further reducing spectral resolution. Nevertheless, both Raman and infrared spectra clearly reveal the formation of γ-FeO(OH) and α-FeO(OH), with γ-FeO(OH) being the dominant phase, in good agreement with the XRD results.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
The flaky FeSiB and FeSiBNbCu amorphous powders used in the experiments were purchased from Qingdao Yunlu Advanced Materials Technology Co., Ltd. (China) and prepared using the airflow crushing method. The subglobular Fe78Si9B13 (prepared by gas-water atomization) and spherical Fe77.3Si6.3B13.9C2.6 (prepared by gas atomization) amorphous powders were purchased from Chengdu Ketailong Alloy Co., Ltd. Pure iron powder was purchased from Hebei Chuangying Metal Materials Co., Ltd. (China) and prepared by the gas atomization method, with Fe content > 99.9 wt%. The reduced iron powder (composition: Fe 98.8, Mn 0.4, Cr 0.2, Si 0.2, S 0.2, Ca 0.1, Al 0.1, wt%) was secondary reduced iron powder, purchased from Tianjin Beichen District Fangzheng Reagent Factory (China). The diatomite (300 mesh, composition: (SiO2) 92.5, (Al2O3) 3.6, (Na2O) 2.7, (Fe2O3) 1.2, wt%) used for the oxygen removal experiments was sourced from Henan Boxu Environmental Protection Technology Co., Ltd. (China). The water used in the experiments was obtained from an ultrapure water system, and the 1% NaCl saline solution was prepared using analytical-grade NaCl (China National Pharmaceutical Group Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.) and ultrapure water.

In the preparation of FePC ribbons, pure iron (>99.95 wt%), ferrophosphorus (22 wt% P), and carbon particles (>99.9 wt%) were weighed according to the nominal composition and melted five times into button ingots using a non-consumable vacuum arc furnace under argon protection. The ingots were then cut and rapidly quenched into ribbons using a vacuum melt-spinner (copper roller speed: 40 m s-1). The amorphous ribbons were vacuum-annealed (pressure < 5 × 10-3 Pa) at 623 K for 1 hour, then ground for 3 min using a commercial grinder and sieved through a 100-mesh screen.

Sample characterization
A Co-source diffractometer (D8 Advance X, Bruker, Germany) and a Cu-source diffractometer (SmartLab, Rigaku, Japan) were used to analyze the phase information of samples. The scanning rates were 10° min-1 and 5° min-1, respectively. The XRD results for the starting metal powders are shown in Supplementary Fig. 27a. HRTEM and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) of the FeSiB powder were performed using a Talos F200x TEM (FEI, USA), with representative HRTEM images shown in Supplementary Fig. 27b. The reaction products were added into 20 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and after filtration through a 0.22 μm filter membrane, the samples containing nano-iron oxide particles were subjected to TEM observation. SEM (GeminiSEM 300, ZEISS, Germany) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer was used for sample observation and analysis. The poorly conductive powders were priorly sputter-coated with platinum. All the SEM observations were repeated three times, yielding similar results. Particle size distributions of the Fe-based MGs, pure iron, and reduced iron powders were measured using a laser particle size analyzer (Mastersizer 3000, Malvern, UK). The BET specific surface area of the samples was tested using a fully automated surface area and porosity analyzer (ASAP 2460, Micromeritics, USA). A Raman spectrometer (LabRAM HR Evolution, Horiba, Japan) and a Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR, RTracer-100, SHIMADZU, Japan) were used to analyze the reaction products. Prior to the FT-IR measurement, the samples were dried at 393 K for 5 min to remove moisture. Compositions on the oxide films of initial and reacted FeSiB samples were measured by an X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Scientific K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher, USA), with charge correction referenced to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. The XAFS spectra of reacted FeSiB and Fe samples were measured at the Energy Materials Beamline (hard branch) of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF) to analyze the oxidation degree and Fe–O coordination environment. For sample preparation, 5 g of the reacted scavenger was vacuum-dried and then milled in a planetary ball mill for 2 hours using a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 6:1. ZrO2 milling balls with a diameter of 5 mm were employed, and 8 mL of ethanol was used as the milling medium. After milling, the powder was dried at 393 K and subsequently sieved through a 400-mesh screen; the collected fine fraction was used for XAFS measurements.

Oxygen removal performance testing
Each oxygen removal experiment was conducted as follows: 0.8 g of diatomite was weighed and added to a 50 mL polypropylene tube, followed by 1 mL of ultrapure water or 1 wt% NaCl solution. The mixture was stirred for 1 min using a polystyrene rod to ensure uniform wetting. Fe-based powder (2 g for rate testing or 0.5 g for capacity testing) was then added and stirred for another minute to ensure thorough mixing. The diatomite dosage of 0.8 g was optimized through preliminary experiments. Routine experiments were conducted at 298 K, while low-temperature experiments were performed at 278 K in a temperature-controlled refrigerator. All measurements for each material were obtained from the same sample, with three samples included in each experimental group, and all experiments exhibited good reproducibility. In the long-term storage experiment, each prepared mixed sample consisting of 2 g of FeSiB powder, 0.8 g of diatomite, and 1 g of saline solution was sealed in a 10 mL centrifuge tube, which was subsequently stored in a vacuum bag. After 30 days, the samples were taken out and subjected to oxygen removal experiments.

The mixed powder was placed in a 70 mm glass Petri dish and immediately transferred to a transparent sealed chamber equipped with an oxygen detector (accuracy: 0.1% VOL, Nanjing Yice Technology Co., Ltd., China). A camera recorded the real-time change in oxygen concentration. When the reading reached 0, the actual oxygen concentration was < 0.05%, corresponding to an oxygen removal efficiency > 99.7%. The sealed chamber had a volume of 560 ± 10 mL for rate testing and 1260 ± 15 mL for capacity testing, measured by water displacement. The Petri dish and detector occupied ~60 ± 5 mL. The recorded videos were analyzed to extract oxygen concentration data over time, enabling evaluation of oxygen removal rate and capacity.

After rate testing, the reacted powders were cleaned by dispersing in 20 mL anhydrous ethanol in a 50 mL beaker, shaking for 20 s, and separating using a magnet. The cleaning process was repeated three times. The powders were then dried on filter paper on a 373 K hot plate for subsequent characterization. In one experiment, the ethanol suspension from washing the FeSiB reaction products was transferred to a 200 mL beaker and left to settle for 1 min. The supernatant was decanted, and the remaining powder was dried at 373 K, yielding iron oxide composite powders with residual diatomite. In the pre-reaction experiment of the FeSiB MG oxygen scavenger, the powder mass was increased from 2.0 to 2.1 g, with all other conditions identical to the standard saline tests. When the oxygen concentration dropped to 15.4%, approximately 0.1 g of FeSiB was fully oxidized, at which point the reaction vessel was opened to restore oxygen levels. To compensate for slight moisture loss during pre-reaction, water was replenished based on the measured weight reduction in the Petri dish before conducting subsequent oxygen removal tests.

DFT calculations
Our spin-polarized first-principles DFT calculations for pure Fe and FeSiB MG were carried out by the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) version 5.4.448-51. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional in the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was employed to describe the exchange-correlation functional52, and the projector augmented-wave (PAW) method with a plane wave basis set was used to model the core-valence electron interactions with an energy cutoff of 500 eV for both calculations. Due to the relatively large simulation cells, the k-points sampling of the first Brillouin zone was carried out using a 2 × 2 × 1 Gamma-centered mesh. To accurately treat the 3d orbitals of Fe atoms, we applied the empirical simplified (rotationally invariant) DFT+U approach with an effective U value (Ueff) of 4.3 eV53-55. The DFT-D3 corrections were used to account for van der Waals interaction56. Electronic self-consistency was achieved when the energy change was less than 10-5 eV. For geometry optimization, the systems were relaxed until the norms of all the forces were smaller than 0.05 eV·Å-1. The BCC Fe slab with the (110) surface exposed was modeled as a BCC structure with 4 layers, and each layer contains 3 × 4 supercells with 2 atoms per supercell (24 atoms per layer). While the Fe-based metallic glass slab with 75 Fe atoms, 12 B atoms and 9 Si atoms was generated using ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) method with NVT ensembles of Nose-Hoover thermostats under 1600 K for 2 ps with a timestep of 2 fs. A vacuum layer of 12 Å in the z direction was added to the slabs to prevent interactions between the neighboring slabs, and two H2O molecules were attached to the surfaces of the slabs in both calculations. Then, one O2 molecule or two O atoms were attached to the surface as the initial state model or final state model in both calculations. The structures of these models were then optimized by the conjugate gradient method. The path and the energy barriers of the O2 adsorption were then calculated using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method, which had been implemented in the VASP transition state tools (VTST)57,58.

The Fe d-band center (εd) was defined as Equation (2):
εd = (∫_{-∞}^{∞} PDOS(ε)·ε·dε) / (∫_{-∞}^{∞} PDOS(ε)·dε) (2)
where PDOS(ε) is the projected density of states of Fe d orbitals and ε is the energy.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a compelling study on Fe-based metallic glasses as ultra-efficient oxygen scavengers. It
addresses long-standing limitations of conventional systems by demonstrating unprecedented oxygen removal rates and
capacities to be further used in gas purification, chemical stabilization, and catalytic processes.
Before publication, there are some improvements needed in the following parts:
1) The V-shaped profile in a saline environment needs to be better explained. Authors have stated that “…the rate drops
sharply in the first 2 hours, then gradually rises. This is likely due to two synergistic effects—NaCl suppresses surface
passivation, and the porous structure enhances reactant transport and active surface exposure.” Authors are strongly
encouraged to perform SEM-EDX or any other surface-sensitive analysis to prove this phenomenon.
2) The experiments were performed on a rather short experimental frame, whereas real applications may require months-
long scavenging activity. The authors need to perform longer-term (e.g., a week) tests with FeSiB MG to ensure that the
material can resist long-term exposure to solvents with acceptable oxygen evolution rates.
3) Theoretical oxygen removal performance was assessed only on Fe content but ignores potential Si contribution, even
though it can enhance the glass forming ability. What is the main reason behind not using Si in the calculations?
4) No elemental mapping was presented to confirm how oxides are distributed. More importantly, a single micrograph was
provided to infer the general morphology, but this may not be so representative. Authors are expected to give a low-
magnification image with elemental mapping and/or indicate diatomite (green) and iron oxide (red) regions
5) Despite the high performance and scalability of Fe-based metallic glasses as oxygen scavengers, translating their
laboratory-scale success into real-world industrial applications poses challenges. Authors are expected to acknowledge this
challenge and present a forward-looking statement on how to address it
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript entitled "Fe-based Metallic Glasses as Ultra-efficient Oxygen Scavengers" claims to report Fe-based
metallic glasses (MGs) with superior oxygen-scavenging performance, exceeding conventional materials by 1–4 orders of
magnitude. While the topic is industrially relevant, the work suffers from several critical flaws. The detailed comments and
suggestions are in below:
1. The authors state that FeSiB MG, pure iron, and reduced iron have "matched volumetric particle sizes" (Supplementary
Fig. 1), but reduced iron exhibits a porous structure with a specific surface area (0.412 m²/g) over 12 times higher than FeSiB
MG (0.0340 m²/g). This drastic difference in surface area—known to dominate reaction kinetics in redox processes—
invalidates direct comparisons of "intrinsic reactivity." Why was reactivity not normalized by surface area to isolate the effect
of amorphous structure?
2. The 48-hour capacity of FeSiB MG (1.596 L/g) is claimed to "surpass the theoretical limit of pure iron (1.566 L/g)". This is
physically implausible unless Si participates in oxygen scavenging, but the authors provide no stoichiometric basis for Si
oxidation (e.g., 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ vs. Si + O₂ → SiO₂). XPS (Supplementary Fig. 2f) shows Si⁴+ but no quantification of
Si-derived oxygen uptake. Without this, the "synergistic activation of Si" remains speculative.
3. The oxygen adsorption energy barrier (1.29 eV for FeSiB vs. 3.39 eV for crystalline Fe) is computed using a static slab
model with 2 H₂O molecules, which fails to replicate the saline/ moist environment of the experiments. Realistic conditions
involve electrolyte (NaCl) and dynamic water layers, which can drastically alter surface energetics. Why were these factors
excluded?
4. XRD identifies γ-FeO(OH) as the primary oxidation product, but Raman spectra (Supplementary Fig. 2e) show no distinct
peaks for this phase, and TEM images of the oxide layer are absent. The claim that γ-FeO(OH) "poorly adheres to the MG
matrix" is unsupported—how was adhesion quantified?
5. Autocatalysis requires a product to accelerate the reaction, but the authors attribute it to "nanoporous γ-FeO(OH) +
diatomite" without kinetic evidence (e.g., rate vs. product concentration plots).
6. The "1–4 orders of magnitude higher rate" (Fig. 2e) compares FeSiB to systems like glucose oxidase and tocopherol,
which operate via entirely different mechanisms (enzymatic vs. redox). A fair comparison would include state-of-the-art Fe-
based scavengers (e.g., nano-Fe@C composites), but these are omitted. Why?
7. Error bars in Figs. 1b,c are small (±0.02%), but the authors report "n=3" without details on reproducibility. Given the high
variability in powder-based reactions, were replicate experiments conducted with different batches of materials?
8. The DFT calculations (page 9) simulate O₂ adsorption on static surfaces with 2 H₂O molecules, ignoring the role of NaCl
electrolyte (critical for enhancing kinetics, Fig. 1c). How do Cl⁻ ions affect O₂ adsorption energy barriers or Fe d-band
centers? Would a more realistic electrolyte-inclusive model alter the proposed atomic-scale mechanism?
9. The manuscript focuses on short-term performance (≤48 hours), but practical applications require long-term stability. Does
FeSiB MG undergo passivation over extended use (e.g., 1 week), and if so, what is the mechanism (e.g., crystalline oxide
layer formation)? Can the scavenger be regenerated (e.g., via reduction) without losing activity?
10. While FeSiB, FePC, and FeSiBC are tested (Supplementary Fig. 9), the correlation between MG composition (e.g.,
B/Si/C content) and oxygen-scavenging performance is unexplored. For instance: Does increasing Si content systematically
enhance capacity, or is there a critical threshold? How do alloying elements (e.g., Nb, Cu in FeSiBNbCu) influence
oxidation kinetics?
11. The experiments are conducted at 298 K, but real-world applications involve variable temperatures/humidity. How does
performance degrade at extreme conditions (e.g., <273 K or >333 K, low relative humidity)? Does the amorphous structure
remain stable under these conditions, or does devitrification occur, altering reactivity?
12. The cost analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3) compares raw material prices but ignores processing costs (e.g., gas
atomization for FeSiB-2). How does scalability (e.g., ton-scale production) affect cost, and can Fe-based MGs compete with
established low-cost scavengers (e.g., reduced iron) in high-volume applications (e.g., food packaging)?
13. The manuscript suggests applications in "gas purification" and "semiconductor manufacturing" (p. 22) but provides no
data on compatibility with these systems. For example: Does the scavenger release toxic byproducts (e.g., B oxides) that
could contaminate semiconductor environments? How does it perform in gas streams with impurities (e.g., CO₂, H₂S)
common in industrial settings?
14. Some suggestions are provided: 1) To validate the Role of Amorphous Structure in Oxygen Adsorption, In-situ X-ray
Absorption Fine Structure (XAFS) should be conducted. comparing Fe’s coordination in amorphous vs. crystalline Fe
before/after reaction would reveal whether the amorphous structure promotes more labile Fe-O bonding, supporting DFT
claims of lower adsorption barriers. 2) Quantifying Si’s Synergistic Oxidation, in-situ Raman Spectroscopy with Isotopic
Labeling should be useful. Using 18O2 instead of ambient 16O2 during reactions, combined with in-situ
Raman, can distinguish O incorporation into Fe oxides vs. Si oxides (via shifted vibrational modes of 18O2-containing species). 3) To
verify Long-Term Stability and Practical Viability, the authors can conduct Operando XRD under Humid/Saline Conditions.
Existing XRD characterizes post-reaction products, but operando XRD would track oxide phase evolution (e.g., γ-FeO(OH)
vs. passivating Fe₃O₄) in real time under moist/saline conditions. 4) To probe the Autocatalysis and Oxide Adhesion, In-situ
Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) with Nanomechanical Mapping can be performed. Measuring the force required to detach
oxide nanoparticles from the MG surface (vs. crystalline Fe) would experimentally validate claims that γ-FeO(OH) “poorly
adheres” to the MG matrix, sustaining active sites.
Given the current work’s focus on applied performance and limited mechanistic depth—coupled with the need for further
validation of core claims, this manuscript may be better suited for journals emphasizing materials applications rather than
fundamental science. Journals such as ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces or Journal of Materials Chemistry A would
provide a more appropriate venue.

Response Letter to Reviewers
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their careful assessment of our manuscript and for
their constructive and insightful comments. We have revised the manuscript extensively in
response, resulting in substantial improvements in both scope and clarity.
In the revised version, the number of figures in the main text has been increased from 4 to
7, and the Supplementary Information has been significantly expanded, with the number of
supplementary figures increasing from 10 to 27. Three additional sections (low-temperature
and long-term storage performance, analysis of oxidation behavior, analysis of the
contribution of Si) have been added to the main text. Owing to space constraints in the main
text, most added data and detailed analyses are presented in the Supplementary Information.
All the revisions in the main text have been marked with yellow background.
The major revisions are summarized below:
 Six new DFT calculations were performed, establishing the high reactivity of Fe and Si
in FeSiB MG under solvation conditions.
 The role of Si was systematically investigated and clarified through a combined DFT–
experimental framework.
 New low-temperature experiments were conducted, demonstrating the unique
performance advantage of FeSiB MG scavenger at low temperature.
 Long-term storage experiments were added, confirming the absence of passivation and
sustained oxygen-scavenging performance for FeSiB.
 Control experiments of samples without diatomite were conducted to exclude potential
interference from the diatomite component.
 Additional XPS, XRD, SEM, TEM, Raman, and FTIR analyses were included to
provide a more comprehensive understanding of the oxidation behavior.
 Synchrotron-based XAFS measurements were introduced to elucidate the Fe–O
coordination environment.
 The previously used color-rendered SEM images illustrating the auto-catalytic behavior
were replaced with corresponding EDS elemental mapping data.
 The characteristic V-shaped oxygen removal behavior of reduced iron powder was
explicitly explained.
 The abstract was shortened to comply with the 150-word limit.
 The “Discussion and Outlook” section was substantially revised to improve clarity and
contextualization.

In the revised paper, we have now performed a comprehensive set of additional DFT

conventional Si materials do not function as effective room-temperature oxygen scavengers.
Nevertheless, in metallurgical processes, the strong oxygen affinity of Si is widely exploited
for the deoxidation of molten steel, highlighting its fundamental thermodynamic driving force
for oxygen removal.
These results clarify that while Fe dominates the practical oxygen removal process, Si
possesses strong intrinsic oxygen affinity and can play a synergistic role in the FeSiB MG. This

Response:
Thank you for this insightful comment. We agree that translating the laboratory-scale
performance of Fe-based MG oxygen scavengers into practical industrial applications remains
a nontrivial challenge. As discussed in the manuscript, the primary bottleneck does not lie in
the intrinsic material design, since Fe-based MGs are compositionally simple and can be
fabricated using well-established rapid solidification routes, but rather in achieving cost-

At present, FeSiB MGs have already been industrialized as soft magnetic materials, with
relatively low raw-material costs; however, their overall price is dominated by processing costs,
9
particularly those associated with melt-spinning. In contrast, the oxygen scavengers proposed
in this work do not require strict control over magnetic properties, ribbon uniformity, or
dimensional consistency, nor do they suffer from yield losses caused by magnetic performance
specifications. These differences provide clear opportunities for process simplification and cost
reduction when the material is repurposed as an oxygen scavenger.
Looking forward, further cost reduction and performance optimization will rely on close
collaboration with the industry to develop scalable, continuous, and application-oriented
fabrication processes. In parallel, extended field testing under realistic service conditions will
be necessary to evaluate long-term stability, system compatibility, and overall cost–benefit
performance.
In the revised manuscript, we have added a forward-looking discussion in the
“Discussion and outlook” section to explicitly address these challenges and the pathways
toward industrial implementation.
Comment 1:
The authors state that FeSiB MG, pure iron, and reduced iron have "matched volumetric
particle sizes" (Supplementary Fig. 1), but reduced iron exhibits a porous structure with a
specific surface area (0.412 m²/g) over 12 times higher than FeSiB MG (0.0340 m²/g). This
drastic difference in surface area—known to dominate reaction kinetics in redox processes—
invalidates direct comparisons of "intrinsic reactivity." Why was reactivity not normalized by
surface area to isolate the effect of amorphous structure?
Response：
Thank you for this thoughtful and technically important comment. We agree that specific
surface area is a key parameter governing reaction kinetics in redox-driven oxygen scavenging.
The surface-area–normalized comparison is carried out and is presented in Fig. 2d of the
original manuscript (shown as Fig. R9 in this response).
Fig. R9. Radar plot comparing FeSiB MG and reduced iron across four normalized metrics: k ,
a
weight-based, cost-based, and surface area-based oxygen removal capacities.
If the oxygen removal performance in Fig. 1 (in the manuscript) were also normalized
by surface area, the apparent advantage of the FeSiB MG would become even more pronounced,
as the newly developed scavenger delivers substantially higher oxygen removal capacity
despite possessing a much lower specific surface area than reduced iron. However, the primary
purpose of Fig. 1 was to present a direct, application-oriented comparison of the practical
oxygen scavenging performance under identical experimental conditions. In this context,
normalizing by surface area would artificially penalize reduced iron—which intrinsically relies
11
on its high porosity and large surface area—and would obscure the real-world performance
differences among the materials.
Therefore, we consider it more appropriate to present the non-normalized experimental
results in Fig. 1 to reflect actual usage performance, while Fig. 2d provides a complementary,
surface-area-normalized analysis to isolate intrinsic reactivity. Taken together, these two
representations allow readers to clearly distinguish between practical scavenging efficiency
and intrinsic material reactivity, and to appreciate the superior performance of FeSiB MG from
both perspectives.
Comment 2:
The 48-hour capacity of FeSiB MG (1.596 L/g) is claimed to "surpass the theoretical limit of
pure iron (1.566 L/g)". This is physically implausible unless Si participates in oxygen
scavenging, but the authors provide no stoichiometric basis for Si oxidation (e.g., 4Fe + 3O₂
→ 2Fe₂O₃ vs. Si + O₂ → SiO₂). XPS (Supplementary Fig. 2f) shows Si⁴+ but no quantification
of Si-derived oxygen uptake. Without this, the "synergistic activation of Si" remains
speculative.
Response:
Thank you for this constructive and insightful comment. We agree that exceeding the
theoretical oxygen removal capacity of pure iron necessarily implies the participation of
additional active elements, and in the revised manuscript we have strengthened both the
theoretical and experimental evidence for the role of Si.
From a theoretical perspective, we have added several new DFT calculations
demonstrating that Si possesses a strong intrinsic oxygen affinity. Although elemental Si is
well known as an effective deoxidizer, it does not normally function as a room-temperature
oxygen scavenger due to rapid surface passivation; for this reason, its deoxidation capability is
primarily exploited in metallurgical processes. The relevant computational details and
analysis are provided in our response to Reviewer 1, Comment 3, and are incorporated into
the revised manuscript.
Experimentally, quantitative analysis of Si oxidation in the original samples was
complicated due to the presence of diatomite, which introduces a significant background in Si
oxidation analysis. To eliminate this interference and directly probe the contribution of Si,
we designed a new set of controlled oxidation experiments in the revised study.
Specifically, 2 g of FeSiB powder was mixed with 30 μL of NaCl solution and allowed to
12
react in air. After 1 h, an additional 30 μL of NaCl solution was added, and this procedure was
repeated multiple times. Samples subjected to n reaction cycles were denoted as FeSiB-Rn.
The use of 30 μL solution per cycle was deliberately chosen to achieve micro-wetting without
full immersion; complete immersion would shift the reaction to a solution-phase oxygen
consumption process, which is inconsistent with both the standard experimental configuration
and practical oxygen scavenger operation. Notably, commercial oxygen scavengers are also
designed to operate under micro-wetting rather than fully submerged conditions, and the
moisture-retaining agent in our standard experiments serves the same purpose.
XPS spectra were collected for samples reacted 10, 20, and 30 times, and the relative
fractions of Si-derived and Fe-derived oxides in the surface oxide layers were quantified and
compared with those of the native oxide film and the nominal alloy composition (Fig. R10).
Two key observations emerge. First, even in the native oxide layer of FeSiB MG, the fraction
of Si oxides is significantly higher than expected from the nominal composition, indicating
preferential oxidation of Si and confirming its strong oxygen affinity, consistent with the
DFT results. Second, as oxidation proceeds, the ratio of Si oxides to Fe oxides increases
monotonically. If Si did not actively participate in oxygen scavenging, progressive oxidation
would lead to Fe-oxide-dominated surfaces and a decreasing relative Si signal. The opposite
trend observed here provides direct and quantitative evidence that Si contributes
substantially to the oxygen removal process.
Taken together, these theoretical and experimental results establish a clear stoichiometric
and mechanistic basis for Si participation in oxygen scavenging, thereby explaining how the

Second, regarding TEM evidence, a new TEM image of the oxidized layer has been added

With respect to adhesion, we emphasize that the statement that γ-FeO(OH) “poorly
adheres to the MG matrix” is not a speculative claim introduced in this work, nor does it rely
on indirect inference alone. Poor adhesion and easy spallation of FeO(OH)-type oxides are
widely recognized and well documented in corrosion science and oxidation literature. This
behavior originates from fundamental crystallographic and physicochemical characteristics of
FeO(OH) rather than from any specific experimental assumption in our study.
Specifically, FeO(OH) is a trivalent iron oxyhydroxide with a relatively simple Fe³⁺
coordination environment and small ionic radius, which promotes anisotropic crystal growth.
As a result, FeO(OH) typically forms platelet-, needle-, or nanoporous microstructures with a
high density of defects and voids. These features lead to discontinuous, mechanically weak
oxide layers that are prone to cracking and exfoliation. In addition, the molar volume expansion
associated with the transformation from metallic Fe to FeO(OH) is significantly larger than
that for Fe O , which promotes stress accumulation at the oxide–metal interface and further
3 4
facilitates delamination.
In contrast, Fe O is a mixed-valence (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) oxide with an inverse spinel structure,
3 4
characterized by dense atomic packing and lower defect density. The presence of Fe²⁺ partially
18
compensates oxygen vacancies during growth, enabling the formation of compact, adherent,
and passivating oxide films. These differences between FeO(OH) and Fe O are extensively
3 4
reported in both classical textbooks and modern studies on iron oxidation and corrosion.
Experimentally, the weak adhesion of γ-FeO(OH) in our system is directly evidenced by
SEM observations after reaction and after mild ultrasonic cleaning, where oxide products are
seen to spontaneously exfoliate from the FeSiB MG surface and form a nanoporous
morphology (see the new Fig. 5b, Fig. 7a, Supplementary Figure 5c, and Fig. R15). Due to
the loose, porous, and mechanically fragile nature of FeO(OH), quantitative adhesion
measurements (e.g., pull-off force determination) are inherently difficult and not commonly
reported even in dedicated corrosion studies.
In summary, the combined XRD, Raman, FTIR, TEM, and SEM results unambiguously
identify γ-FeO(OH) as the primary oxidation product, and both fundamental materials
chemistry and direct morphological evidence support its poor adhesion relative to compact
oxides such as Fe O . This behavior underpins the continuous exposure of fresh reactive sites
3 4
and is therefore fully consistent with the observed oxidation kinetics and autocatalytic
characteristics discussed in this work.

We appreciate your insightful comment regarding the long-term stability and practical

Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully agree that alloy
composition—such as B/Si/C contents—and multicomponent alloying (e.g., Nb and Cu in
FeSiBNbCu alloys) can play an important role in oxidation and oxygen-scavenging behavior,
and that this topic deserves systematic investigation. However, two practical scientific
constraints limit a comprehensive discussion within the scope of the present work.
First, the glass-forming ability (GFA) imposes a strong compositional constraint. In
Fe-based MGs, elements such as Si and B simultaneously govern both chemical reactivity and
GFA. Deviating either above or below an optimal Si (or B) content can readily induce partial
or full crystallization, as illustrated in Fig. R18 below. As a result, systematically varying Si
content while strictly maintaining a fully amorphous structure—and thereby establishing a
clear “threshold” relationship between composition and oxygen-scavenging performance—is
experimentally challenging.

Second, in higher-order systems such as FeSiBNbCu, the underlying mechanisms
become substantially more complex. Coupled effects among multiple alloying elements can
simultaneously influence oxidation kinetics, passive film structure, and local chemical
environments. Disentangling the individual contributions of Nb, Cu, or other elements would
require extensive, dedicated studies that go well beyond the scope of the present manuscript.
Despite these limitations, we fully acknowledge the scientific importance of these
questions and intend to address them in future work. The primary objective of the current study
is to elucidate the fundamental oxygen-scavenging behavior and unique mechanistic features
25
of a representative FeSiB MG system. Accordingly, a broader, composition–performance
mapping was not pursued here. We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestion,
which will help guide our future research directions.
Comment 11:
The experiments are conducted at 298 K, but real-world applications involve variable
temperatures/humidity. How does performance degrade at extreme conditions (e.g., <273 K
or >333 K, low relative humidity)? Does the amorphous structure remain stable under these
conditions, or does devitrification occur, altering reactivity?
Response:
Thank you for this professional and important suggestion. The effects of humidity and
temperature on performance are addressed as follows.
The Fe-based MG oxygen scavenger developed in this study is a water-rich composite
system. In the standard experimental configuration, it consists of 2 g of FeSiB powder, 0.8 g
of diatomite, and 1 g of water. The water content in the system is excessive for oxygen-
scavenging reactions. Therefore, fluctuations in ambient humidity have a negligible
effect on its oxygen-scavenging performance. The performance of a few commercial
oxygen scavengers is somewhat influenced by humidity; however, their systems are
fundamentally different from ours and are beyond the scope of this study.
In practical applications, Fe-based oxygen scavengers are typically used within a
temperature range of 15–30 °C (288–303 K). For conventional Fe powder-based scavengers,
low temperature severely suppresses reaction kinetics, and their oxygen-removal capability
becomes weak below 10 °C (283 K).
Regarding high-temperature conditions, we attempted experiments at 55 °C (328 K).
However, at this temperature the water-retaining agent (diatomite) was unable to effectively
retain water, leading to rapid evaporation. This not only disrupted the core reaction
environment required for oxygen scavenging but also caused damage to the oxygen sensor,
preventing reliable high-temperature measurements.
To evaluate low-temperature adaptability, we conducted comparative experiments at 5 °C
(278 K). As shown in Fig. R19, the oxygen-scavenging efficiency of conventional reduced
iron powder decreases dramatically under these conditions, removing only ~50% of the oxygen
within 24 h, which is insufficient for applications such as food and pharmaceutical preservation.
In contrast, the Fe-based MG scavenger maintains a high oxygen-removal rate and is able to
fully consume oxygen in sealed containers within a much shorter time, thereby overcoming
26
the low-temperature limitation of traditional scavengers.
We also explored an extreme low-temperature condition of -10 °C (263 K, below the
freezing point). Due to the water-containing nature of the system, the composite rapidly freezes
at this temperature, and the oxygen-scavenging reaction effectively ceases (Fig. R20). This
indicates that such water-assisted scavengers are not suitable for sub-freezing environments.
Overall, these results demonstrate that Fe-based MG scavengers exhibit significantly
superior oxygen-removal performance compared with conventional materials under room
temperature and non-freezing low-temperature conditions.
In the revised manuscript, we added a dedicated section entitled “Low-temperature and
long-term storage performance” to specifically discuss the low-temperature performance of
the FeSiB oxygen scavenger.

The cost analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3) compares raw material prices but ignores processing

Response：
Thank you for this important comment. We agree that processing cost and scalability are
critical factors for real-world implementation, and we clarify these points below.
First, we would like to clarify that the previous Supplementary Fig. 3 and the associated
cost analysis are based specifically on the low-cost, flake-type FeSiB MG, rather than on
other Fe-based MG compositions or high-cost processing routes. Importantly, the estimated
cost already includes the major processing expenses. The cost breakdown is as follows: the raw
material cost is approximately 3,800 CNY per ton, while the core processing and auxiliary
costs are estimated at 4,000–4,700 CNY per ton. This results in a total estimated large-scale
cost of ~7,800–8,500 CNY per ton (7.8–8.5 CNY per kg). These values were discussed with
industrial partners and are representative of current conditions in China; all prices quoted refer
to the Chinese market.
Regarding scalability (ton-scale and above), it is necessary to distinguish between
different application requirements. In China, soft-magnetic FeSiB MG ribbons are already
produced at a very large scale (annual production exceeding 100,000 tons). Such materials
must meet stringent requirements for magnetic properties and compositional uniformity, which
necessitate high raw-material purity, strict process control, and inevitably generate scrap,
resulting in a current market price of ~13,000 CNY per ton (with actual production cost being
lower). In contrast, Fe-based MGs used as oxygen scavengers do not require magnetic
performance, dimensional uniformity, or ribbon integrity. Their sole functional requirement is
oxygen-scavenging activity. Consequently, raw-material pretreatment and process control can
be significantly simplified, and the scrap rate can be reduced to a very low level, leading to
substantially lower overall production costs at scale.
With respect to competitiveness in high-volume applications such as food packaging, Fe-
28
based MG scavengers can offset their higher unit price through superior kinetics and efficiency.
Specifically, complete oxygen removal by FeSiB MG can be achieved in less than one quarter
of the time required for reduced iron powder, enabling rapid establishment of an oxygen-free
environment and improved preservation performance, particularly for oxygen-sensitive foods
and pharmaceuticals. Moreover, the 12 h and 24 h oxygen-removal capacities of FeSiB are
approximately 2–3 times higher than those of reduced iron powder, meaning that only one-
third to one-half of the material mass is required to achieve the same preservation effect.
Even when comparing the upper-bound cost of FeSiB (~8.5 CNY per kg) with the lower-
bound cost of reduced iron powder used in scavengers (~6 CNY per kg), the cost per unit
oxygen removed is estimated to be ~2.8–4.2 CNY for FeSiB, versus ~6 CNY for reduced iron.
Therefore,when evaluated on a performance-normalized basis, Fe-based MG scavengers
retain a clear cost advantage and are well positioned to compete in large-scale, cost-sensitive
applications such as food packaging. We have discussed this issue in the “Discussion and
outlook” section of the revised manuscript.
